pages.title: Introduction to time complexity
pages.content:
Time complexity is a way to measure how long an algorithm takes to run as the amount of **input data** increases. Think of it as a method for figuring out how **fast or slow** an algorithm is.

There are multiple ways to measure time complexity of an algorithm:
1. Best case
2. Average case
3. Worst case

We will focus on understanding the **worst-case scenario** of how an algorithm performs. We use a special notation called “Big O notation” to talk about worst-case time complexity.

#### Why is Time Complexity important?
Time complexity of an algorithm is independent from the machine the algorithm is going to run on. Understanding time complexity is important because it gives us a way of **comparing algorithms** without worrying about the system on which the algorithms are going to run.

pages.title: Finding time complexity - Rule 1
pages.content:
To find out time complexity of an algorithm, we look at the number of operations performed based on the input size.

Let's take a look at the below code:
```python
a = 1
b = 2
print(a + b)
```

In the above algorithm, there is no input. In total three operations are being performed in three lines. Every single operation is denoted as O(1) (pronounced as Big O of 1).

Thus, for the above example, we have time complexity as `O(1) + O(1) + O(1) = 3 * O(1)`

But we denote the time complexity of the above algorithm as O(1), ignoring the constant 3.

#### Rule 1 - Ignore the constants
When calculating time complexity, we ignore the constant values because they don’t matter when the input size becomes large.

Thus O(1), 5 * O(1), 8 * O(1) are all O(1)

### Task
What will be the time complexity of this algorithm?

```python

print(a)
```

pages.title: Finding time complexity - O(N)
pages.content:
Let's look at another algorithm now.
```python
for i = 0 to N
    print(i)
```

In the above algorithm, we are running a loop from 0 to N. In total the loop will run **N** times. For each iteration of the loop we are doing one operation `print(i).

The final time complexity will be: N * O(1) => O(N).

This time the algorithm dependent on a variable N and with that the time complexity also has the value N.

### Task

What if we were doing two operations inside the loop?
```python
for i = 0 to N
    print(i)
    print(i * 2)
```

pages.title: Finding time complexity - Rule 2
pages.content:
Let's see a different example now.

```python
a = 4 + 5
for i = 0 to N
    print(a)
```

Can you determine the time complexity of this algorithm?

Time complexity of first line => O(1)
Time complexity of the loop => O(N)

Total time complexity => O(1) + O(N).

But can we use two Big Os to define time complexity of an algorithm?
Nope

#### Rule 2 - Focus only on the largest factor
If an algorithm has multiple different parts with different time complexity, when determining the final time complexity we only look at the largest factor.

Because the biggest factor will slow down an algorithm the most.

Thus the time complexity of the above algorithm will be: **O(N)**

### Task

```python

    print(i)

for j = 0 to N
    print(j)
```

pages.title: Finding time complexity - Nested loops
pages.content:
Let's take a bit complex algorithm now.
```python
for i = 0 to N
    for j = 0 to N
        print(i)
        print(j)
```

What do you think will the time complexity be?

This is a nested loop. The outer loop runs N times. And for each iteration of the outer loop, the inner loop also runs N times.

For each iterations of inner loop there are two operations.

Complexity of line 3 and 4 => O(1) + O(1) => **O(1)**

Total complexity of inner loop => N * (complexity of line 3 and 4) => N * O(1) => **O(N)**

Total complexity of outer loop => N * (complexity of line 2 - 4) => N * O(N) => **O(N * N)**

It can also be represented as **O(N ^ 2)**

Notice how the number of operations are multiplied in case of nested codes.

### Task
Now can you find the complexity of this algorithm?
```python
for i = 0 to N
    for j = 0 to N
        for k = 0 to N
            print(i)
```

We also learned about two rules of finding time complexity of an algorithm

We also learned how to calculate time complexity of nested loops.

In the next lesson we will see how we have to break the Rule 2 sometimes and also how to apply time complexity to DSA problems in general.

pages.title: Time complexity for DSA
pages.content:
We will solve a lot of examples on time complexity, but let’s take a break and think about the applications of time complexity when it comes to solving DSA problems.

Remember how each problem statement on SEED-IT has a **Constraints** section. This section talks about the constraint on the size of input given to you.

The constraints section generally look like this:  
$1 \leq N \leq 10^5$

This means that the value of N can range from 1 to 10^5.

----

For harder problems it is not enough that your solution is correct, it also has to be efficient enough to run within the given time limit.

In general, you can assume that the current day computers can run up to 10 ^ 8 operations per second. You can calculate the worst case time complexity of your algorithm and check if the total number of operations are beyond 10 ^ 8. If the operations performed by your algorithm exceeds 10 ^ 8, you will get TLE or Time limit exceeded.

pages.title: Time complexity of standard algorithms
pages.content:
Hope you have got an idea on how to figure out whether your algorithm will work or give TLE based on the constraints provided.

The steps are - 
1. Find the worst case time complexity of your algorithm
2. Put the maximum possible value of N according to the constraints and check the approximate number of operations
3. If the operations are below $10 ^ 8$, your algorithm can run otherwise it will give TLE.

---

Let's now look at time complexity of some of the standard algorithms. Remembering this numbers help you quickly decide whether you can do that operation or not based on the constraints.

### Loops
| Algorithm | Complexity | Max value of N possible | 
|---------- |----------|----------|
| Single loop till N | $O(N)$ | $10 ^ 8$ |
| Nested loops both till N | $O(N ^ 2)$ | $10 ^ 4$ |
| Two loops one by one till N | $O(N)$ | $10 ^ 8$ |


### Searching
| Algorithm | Complexity | Max value of N possible | 
|---------- |----------|----------|
| Linear search | $O(N)$ | $10 ^ 8$ |
| Binary search | $O(log N)$ | $10 ^ {10 ^ 8}$ |


### Sorting
| Algorithm | Complexity | Max value of N possible | 
|---------- |----------|----------|
| Bubble sort, insertion sort | $O(N ^ 2)$ | $10 ^ 4$ |
| Merge sort | $O(N log N)$ | $10 ^ 7$ |


### Array or list operations
| Algorithm | Complexity |
|---------- |----------|
| Adding an element at the end of a list | $O(1)$ |
| Adding an element at the start of a list | $O(N)$ |
| Counting the occurrences of a number in an array | $O(N)$ |

pages.title: Log N time complexity
pages.content:
Till now we have seen time complexity of loops which run linearly from 1 to N, thus having approximately N number of operations. Even if we are incrementing $i$ by 1, 2 or 10, the constant doesn't really matter.

But there are certain types of loops which do very few operations than N and thus we need other ways to denote their time complexity.

Look at the below code for an example
```python
i = 1
while i <= n:
    print(i)
    i *= 2
```

Here $i$ is getting doubled in each iteration.

For $n = 4$, the iterations will be
```python
1
2
4
```
Only 3 iterations. 

How about $n = 16$?
```python
1
2
4
8
16
```
Only 5 iterations.

**Can we calculate the total number of iterations for any $n$?**  
In each iteration, $i$ is getting doubled, so the values of $i$ will be
$1, 2, 4, 8, \ldots, n$.

If we can count the total number of values of $i$, we will know the time complexity. This is because time complexity is nothing but a measure of the number of operations in an algorithm.

**Now, how do we calculate the total number of iterations?**  
If you observe, all the values of $i$ are of the form $2^x$.  
$2^0, 2^1, 2^2, 2^3, \ldots, 2^x$

The last value will be less than or equal to $n$.

In the above series, we can see, in total, there are $x + 1$ values. Thus, we can say, that there were $x + 1$ iterations of the loop.

**How do we find $x$ then?**  

We know that $2^x \leq n$  

Taking the logarithm on both sides.

$\log_2(2^x) \leq \log_2(n)$  

$\log_2(2^x) \equiv xlog_2(2)$   
$\log_2(2)$ is $1$.

Thus, the equation becomes:  
$x \leq \log_2(n)$

The maximum possible value for $x$ is $\log_2(n)$, and $x$ denotes the maximum number of times the loop will run. Thus, the time complexity of this algorithm will be $\log_2(n)$, as figured out by the total number of operations done in the loop.

----

In general, you can remember that anytime a variable in loop is multiplied by a number greater than 1, the time complexity of the loop will be of the form: $log(n)$.

### Task

```python

while i <= n:
    print(i)
    i *= 3
```

pages.title: Square root N time complexity
pages.content:
Now that we have learned about $log(N)$ time complexity, there is only one other non-linear time complexity which is important to know: $O(sqrt(N))$.

That is the number of operations of an algorithm is approximately $sqrt(N)$.

This is an example of a code with $O(sqrt(n))$ time complexity.
```python
i = 1
while i * i <= n:
    print(i)
    i += 1
```

In this, even though $i$ is incremented by 1 in each iteration, the value of $i$ has to go only till $i * i <= n$.


#### How do we calculate the total number of times the loop is running?
It's simple. The iterations will be: $1, 2, 3, 4, 5, \ldots, x$, until $(x *x) \leq n$.

**Let's solve for $x$:**

Given the condition $x^2 \leq n$, we aim to find the value of $x$ that satisfies this inequality.

1. **Initial inequality:**  
   $x^2 \leq n$

2. **Taking the square root on both sides:**  
   $\sqrt{x^2} \leq \sqrt{n}$

3. **Simplifying:**  
   $x \leq \sqrt{n}$

Thus, the maximum possible value of $x$ can be $\sqrt{n}$, making it the time complexity of the given algorithm.

   j = 0
   while j * j <= n:

      j = j + 1

pages.title: Introduction to Space complexity
pages.content:
Space complexity refers to the amount of **memory or space** an algorithm requires to run as a function of the **input data size**. Alongside time complexity, it is an important aspect of analyzing an algorithm's efficiency.

#### Key Points:

**Space Complexity = Auxiliary Space + Input Space:** This means we consider both the extra memory needed by the algorithm and the memory required for the input data.

**Memory Usage:** This includes the memory for variables, data structures, and function calls.

**Auxiliary Space:** This is the extra memory the algorithm uses, excluding the input data. We mainly focus on this because the input size is usually fixed.

**Big O Notation:** We use this to describe the worst-case space usage of an algorithm.

#### Why It Matters?

Understanding space complexity helps prevent memory issues and ensures that algorithms work efficiently, especially when dealing with large data or limited resources.

pages.title: Finding space complexity
pages.content:
To determine an algorithm's space complexity, we examine the amount of extra memory used based on the input size.

Let's take a look at the following code:
```cpp
int a = 1
int b = 2
cout << a + b;
```
The above algorithm declares two variables *a* and *b*. Each variable takes constant space, which is independent of the input size. Every single variable takes **O(1)** space.

Thus, for the above example, we have the space complexity as:

**O(1) + O(1) = 2 * O(1)**

However, we denote the above algorithm's space complexity as **O(1)**, ignoring the constant 2.

**Ignore the constants**
When calculating space complexity, we ignore the constant values because they don’t matter when the input size becomes large.

**Examine the code below:**
```cpp
cout << "Hello";
```

pages.title: Understanding Space Complexity of Algorithms
pages.content:
When analyzing space complexity, we focus on the amount of memory that an algorithm or data structure requires about the size of the input. The space can be categorized into **input space** (the space taken up by the input data) and **auxiliary space** (the extra memory used by the algorithm for computation).

#### Space Complexity of Common Algorithms
|  *Algorithms*   | *Auxiliary Space* | *Input Space* |
| -------------   | -------------     | -----------   |
| Linear Search   |      O(1)         |    O(n)       |
| Binary Search   |      O(1)         |    O(n)       |
| Selection Sort  |      O(1)         |    O(n)       |
| Bubble Sort     |      O(1)         |    O(n)       |
| Insertion Sort  |      O(1)         |    O(n)       |
| Merge Sort      |      O(n)         |    O(n)       |
| Quick Sort      |      O(log n)     |    O(n)       |
| Radix Sort      |      O(n+k)       |    O(n)       |
| Counting Sort   |      O(n+m)       |    O(n)       |
| Heap Sort       |      O(1)         |    O(n)       |
| Bucket Sort     |      O(n)         |    O(n)       |

- Quicksort has a space complexity of O(log(n)) in the average case. It can be O(n) due to an unbalanced partitioning leading to a deep recursion stack in the worst case.
- k is the range of input in Radix sort.
- Counting Sort requires O(N+M), where N and M are the space taken by outputArray[] and countArray[] respectively.

pages.title: Trade-Off
pages.content:
#### The trade-off between space and time complexity:
It is basically a problem-solving technique in which we solve a problem :
- Either in less time and using more space, or
- In very little space by spending more time.

The trade-offs between time and space complexity are often *inversely proportional*, meaning that improving one may worsen the other.

The best algorithm is the one that helps to solve a problem that requires less space in memory as well as takes less time to generate the output. But in general, it is not always possible to achieve both of these conditions at the same time.

If a problem is slow but memory-efficient, using more memory can speed it up. Conversely, if a solution is fast but memory-intensive, using less memory might slow it down.

**Example:**  
- Selection sort uses o(n^2) time complexity but no auxiliary space. Space complexity o(1)
- But merge sort uses o(n log n) time complexity and extra O(n) space.

pages.title: Average Flex
pages.content:
Averages can also be searched with binary search. For a candidate average `x`, subtract `x` from every element. The question becomes whether any length-K window has a transformed sum of at least zero.

If a feasible window exists, the true maximum average is at least `x`, so search higher. Otherwise search lower. This monotonic feasibility test allows binary search on a real-valued answer.

pages.title: Coins And Triangle
pages.content:
A triangle of height `H` needs `H(H+1)/2` coins. As `H` increases, the required number of coins never decreases, so feasibility is monotonic.

Binary-search the largest feasible height:
- `H` is feasible when `H(H+1)/2 <= N`.
- If a midpoint is feasible, move right to try a larger height.
- Otherwise move left.

This is a classic example of binary search on the answer.

- This array is increasing

Also, we can use an implicit array, because we can find f(r) very quickly. So instead of having an array, we'll just have a function which returns f(r).

Now, how do we find the last index such that f(r) <= n?

pages.title: Introduction to GCD and LCM
pages.content:
**GCD (Greatest Common Divisor)** and **LCM (Least Common Multiple)** are fundamental concepts in number theory and mathematics. They are used to find relationships between two or more numbers and play a significant role in various mathematical computations and problem-solving.


**GCD**

The GCD of two or more integers is the largest positive integer that divides each of the given numbers without leaving a remainder. In other words, it is the greatest common factor shared by the numbers. GCD is often denoted by the symbol "gcd(a, b)" or simply "(a, b)". 
For example to : 
The GCD of { $34, 56$ } is $2$ 
The GCD of { $64, 96$ } is $32$  
**GCD** is also known as **Highest Common Factor** **( HCF )** 



**LCM**

The LCM of two or more integers is the smallest positive integer that is divisible by each of the given numbers. It is the least common multiple shared by the numbers. LCM is often denoted by the symbol "lcm(a, b)" or simply "[a, b]".
For example to : 
The LCM of { $34, 56$ } is  $952$ 
The LCM of { $64, 96$ } is  $192$

pages.title: GCD - LCM Relationship
pages.content:
**GCD** AND **LCM** of two numbers $a$ and $b$ are related to each other by a mathematical relation, 
$$ GCD (a,b) * LCM (a,b) = a*b $$ 
**Proof :** 
Let's consider two numbers, $a$ and $b$, with their prime factorizations:

$$a = {p_1}^{x_1} {p_2}^{x_2} \cdots {p_k}^{x_k}$$ 
But as opposed to the usual prime factorization that we've seen, here, we will consider the prime factors of both $a$ and $b$, and not just the prime factors of $a$. Wherever $p_k$ is a prime factor of $b$, but not a prime factor of $a$, we will just set $$ {x_k}$$ to be $0$. Now, since $a^0 = 1$, this is still a valid prime factorization, but just with some extra redundant factors thrown in.


Similarly, let
$$b = {p_1}^{y_1} {p_2}^{y_2} \cdots {p_k}^{y_k}$$  
where $$ {y_k}$$ is $0$ for every prime factor which is not a factor of $b$ but is a factor of $a$.

The prime factorization of $GCD(a,b)$ would include all the common prime factors of $a$ and $b$, each raised to the minimum exponent present in either factorization as it should be a divisor of both $a$ and $b$.

Thus, we get that : 
$GCD ( a,b ) = $ $${p_1}^{min(x_1,y_1)} {p_2}^{min(x_2,y_2)} \cdots {p_k}^{min(x_k,y_k)}$$ and 

The prime factorization of $LCM(a,b)$ includes all the prime factors of $a$ and $b$, each raised to the maximum exponent present in either factorization as it should be a multiple of both $a$ and $b$.

Thus, $LCM ( a,b ) = $ $${p_1}^{max(x_1,y_1)} {p_2}^{max(x_2,y_2)} \cdots {p_k}^{max(x_k,y_k)}$$ 

We also note that $max(x, y) + min(x, y) = x + y$, for any $x$ and $y$. So thus, $LCM(a,b) * GCD(a,b)$ will equal to 

$$GCD(a,b) * LCM(a,b) = {p_1}^{x_1+y_1} {p_2}^{x_2+y_2} \cdots {p_k}^{x_k+y_k}$$  
and $a*b$ equals to 
$$ a* b = {p_1}^{x_1+y_1} {p_2}^{x_2+y_2} \cdots {p_k}^{x_k+y_k}$$  hence we can can conclude that  
$$ GCD (a,b) * LCM (a,b) = a*b $$ 

**The LCM can be calculated with the GCD
using this property:**

$$\operatorname{lcm}(a, b) = \frac{a \cdot b}{\gcd(a, b)}$$


**Warning!**
Coding $\text{lcm}$ as a * b / gcd(a, b) might cause integer overflow if the
value of a * b is greater than the max size of the data type of a * b (e.g.
the max size of int in C++ and Java is around $2 * 10^9$ ).
Dividng a by gcd(a, b) first, then multiplying it by b will prevent
integer overflow if the result fits in an int.

pages.title: Euclids Time Quest
pages.content:
We saw how to compute $\gcd(a, b)$, where $a \geq b$. But how much does it take? Let us try to count the number of steps that the algo takes.

**Claim 1:**\
$a \% b \leq \frac{a}{2}$.

**Proof:**
- Case 1: If $b \leq \frac{a}{2}$, then, since $a \% b  \frac{a}{2}$, then $a \% b$ is just $a - b$ (since we can't subtract $b$ twice from $a$), which is at most $\frac{a}{2}$. So, in this case also, we again have $a \% b \leq \frac{a}{2}$.

Thus, the claim is proved.

---

Now, let us see the first two steps of the Euclid's algo:
- We have $(a, b)$, which gets converted into $(b, a\%b)$.
- We have $(b, a\%b)$, which gets converted into $(a\%b, b \% (a\%b))$.

So after two steps, the largest number, which was $a$ has become $a\%b$ in the current pair, which as we have shown is $\leq \frac{a}{2}$.\
Thus, in two steps, we have reduced the larger number by at least half. So, in at most $2 * \log_2{a}$ steps, we will hit $0$.\
Thus, the time complexity of this algorithm is $O(log(a))$.

pages.title: Modular Arithmetic
pages.content:
**In modular arithmetic**, instead of working directly with the integers themselves, we work with their
remainders when divided by another integer $m$, we call this integer as modulo $m$ or this operating as taking modulo $m$. For example, if we take $m = 21$, then instead of working with x = $247$, we use $x$ mod $21$ = $16$, 
$247$ mod $21$ is $16$ due to the remainder left when $247$ is divided by $21$. 
Usually, m will be a large prime, given in the problem; the two most common values are $10^9 + 7$, and $998 244 353$.
Modular arithmetic is used to avoid dealing with numbers that overflow built-in data types,
because we can take remainders.


The mathematical binary operations in Modular arithmetic transform to :

$$(a+b) \bmod m = (a \bmod m + b \bmod m) \bmod m$$

$$(a-b) \bmod m = (a \bmod m - b \bmod m) \bmod m$$

$$(a \cdot b) \pmod{m} = ((a \bmod m) \cdot (b \bmod m)) \bmod m$$

$$a^b \bmod {m} = (a \bmod m)^b \bmod m$$ 

**Warning :** 
It's important to note that when working with modular arithmetic, raising a number to a power and then taking the modulus is not the same as taking the modulus of individual components before raising to the power. In other words, In other words, $a^b$ mod $m$ is not as same as $(a \mod m)^{b \mod m}$

pages.title: ModInverse
pages.content:
**Modular Multiplicative Inverse**

Modular multiplicative inverse of an integer  
$a$  is an integer  
$x$  such that  
$a \cdot x$  is congruent to  
$1$  modular some modulus  
$m$ . To write it in a formal way: we want to find an integer  
$x$  so that

 
$$a \cdot x \equiv 1 \mod m.$$ 
We will also denote  
$x$  simply with  
$a^{-1}$ .

We should note that the modular inverse does not always exist. For example, let  
$m = 4$ ,  
$a = 2$ .
We will check all possible values of $x$ modulo $4$ and see if any of them satisfy the equation $2*x ≡ 1$(mod 4)
- $x = 0 : 2 * 0 ≡ 0 ≠ 1 (mod\  4) $
- $x = 1 : 2 * 1 ≡ 2 ≠ 1 (mod\  4) $
- $x = 2 : 2 * 2 ≡ 4 ≠ 1 (mod\  4) $
- $x = 3 : 2 * 3 ≡ 6 ≠ 1 (mod\  4) $

By checking all possible values modulo  
$m$ , it should become clear that we cannot find  
$a^{-1}$  satisfying the above equation. It can be proven that the modular inverse exists if and only if  
$a$  and  
$m$  are relatively prime (i.e.  
$\gcd(a, m) = 1$ ).

If we know $m$ is prime, then we can also use [Fermat’s little theorem](https://mathworld.wolfram.com/FermatsLittleTheorem.html) (explained next) to find the inverse. 

$a^{m−1} ≡1 (mod m)$

If we multiply both sides with $a-1$, we get 

$a^{-1} ≅ a^ {m-2} (mod m)$

It can also be converted into different states that $a^{p-1}-1$ is an integer multiple of p. 

- $a^{p-1} ≡ 1$ (mod p) or $a^{p-1}$ % p = 1

Taking example to understand how fermat's little theorem works.
 - P = an integer Prime number   
 - a = an integer which is not multiple of P  
 - Let a = 2 and P = 19 
 
 According to Fermat's little theorem 
 - $2^{19 - 1}$  ≡  1 mod(19)
 We got  262144 % 19 ≡ 1   
 which means (262144-1) is a multiple of 19.

We can find inverse using fermat's little theorem
According to fermat' litte theorem 
- $a^{m-1}$ = 1 (mod m)

Multiplying both side by $a^{-1}$
- $a^{-1}$ ≡ $a^{m-2}$ (mod m)

pages.title: Combinatorics
pages.content:
Combinatorics is the mathematics of counting and arranging. Of course, most people know how to count, but combinatorics applies mathematical operations to count quantities that are much too large to be counted the conventional way.

In the following modules we will learn about Combinatorics and how these concepts are used in Competitive Programming. 

Counting Theory is the set of systematic rules to count, most of these are very intuitive and you might've even used in real life without realizing it.

pages.title: MCQ - City Path Combinatorics Problem
pages.content:
Consider you are at a city - $S$ and you want to go to city - $D$. \
There are two intermediate cities - $A$ and $B$. 

You can travel from $S$ to $A$ by taking one of the three paths.
And, travel from $S$ to $B$ by taking one of the two paths. 



How many number of total ways are there to reach $D$ from $S$?

callout.title: Key takeaway
callout.text: Focus on the core idea in MCQ - City Path Combinatorics Problem and choose an implementation that remains correct on edge cases and within the stated complexity.

pages.title: Rule of Sum
pages.content:
The way you counted the number of paths in the previous problem is called the ***Rule of Sum***. 

Formally, if there are $A$ ways of doing a task and $B$ ways of doing another task and both are dependant on each other - you can either perform the first task or the second task then there are $A$ $+$ $B$ total ways.

This can be extended to more than 2 tasks. \
In general if there are $N$ tasks and there are $A_i$ ways of doing the $i$-th task and you can perform exactly one task at a time, then there are $\sum_{i=1}^N A_i$ total number of ways.

**Note:** Sigma notation is a method used to express a long sum in a concise way. 

$\sum_{i=1}^NA_i$ = $A_1$ + $A_2$ + $A_3$ ..... + $A_N$

callout.text: Focus on the core idea in Rule of Sum and choose an implementation that remains correct on edge cases and within the stated complexity.

pages.title: MCQ - City Pathways Combinatorics Challenge II
pages.content:
Consider you are at a city - $S$ and you want to go to city - $D$. \
There are two intermediate cities - $A$ and $B$. 

You can travel from $S$ to $A$ by taking one of the three paths.
And, travel from $A$ to $B$ by taking one of the two paths.

From $B$ there exist one path go to $D$ 



How many number of total ways are there to reach $D$ from $S$?

callout.title: Key takeaway
callout.text: Focus on the core idea in MCQ - City Pathways Combinatorics Challenge II and choose an implementation that remains correct on edge cases and within the stated complexity.

pages.title: Rule of product
pages.content:
The way you counted the number of paths in the previous problem is called the ***Rule of Product***. 

Formally, if there are $A$ ways to perform one task and $B$ ways to perform a second task, and these tasks can be done independently of each other, then the total number of ways to perform both tasks is $A$ $\cdot$ $B$


In the previous example, no matter the path you choose for $A$, there always existed 2 paths from $A$ to $B$ - so these two actions were independent.

Again, this can be extended to more than 2 tasks. 

So, if we have $N$ independent tasks and $i$-th task can be performed in $A_i$ then there are $\prod_{i=1}^N A_i$ number of ways to perform all the tasks.


**Note:**: Product notation (also called pi notation) indicates repeated multiplication.

$\prod_{i=1}^N A_i$ = $A_1$ x $A_2$ x $A_3$......x $A_N$

callout.title: Key takeaway
callout.text: Focus on the core idea in Rule of product and choose an implementation that remains correct on edge cases and within the stated complexity.

pages.title: Modular Arithmetic Basics
pages.content:
While counting, the Rule of product, sum might produce a very large output. \
So, many problems ask the output, modulo a constant number (usually a large prime). 

You might need these basic modular arithmetic identities going forward.
- $(A + B)$ mod $M$ $=$ $((A$ mod $M)$ $+$ $(B$ mod $M))$ mod $M$.
- $(A \cdot B)$ mod $M$ $=$ $((A$ mod $M)$ $\cdot$ $(B$ mod $M))$ mod $M$.
- $(A^B)$ mod $M$ $=$ $((A$ mod $M)^B)$ mod $M$

Also, $(A - B)$ mod $M$ is equal to 
- $((A$ mod $M)$ $-$ $(B$ mod $M))$ mod $M$ if $A$ mod $M$ is greater than $B$ mod $M$.
- $(((A$ mod $M)$ $-$ $(B$ mod $M)) + M)$ mod $M$ if $A$ mod $M$ is smaller than $B$ mod $M$.


Note that the second condition of subtraction can replace the first one too, but **not** vice-verse.

Also, many time we need to use _modular multiplicative inverse_. Learn more about that here.

If we have two sets $A$ and $B$.

- $A \cup B$ is the set that contains all the elements that belong to $A$ or $B$ or to both of them.
- $|A|$ is the size of the set $A$.
- A set $B$ is a subset of set $A$ if all the elements in $B$ also belong so $A$.

The Inclusion-Exclusion principle helps to count the size of union of two sets say - $A$, $B$. 

Symbolically we can represent it as - \

3. $|A|$ $-$ $|B|$ $-$ $|C|$ $+$ $|A \cap B|$ $+$ $|B \cap C|$ $+$ $|A \cap C|$ $-$ $|A \cap B \cap C|$
4. $|A|$ $+$ $|B|$ $+$ $|C|$ $-$ $|A \cap B|$ $+$ $|B \cap C|$ $-$ $|A \cap C|$ $-$ $|A \cap B \cap C|$

pages.content: How many permutations of size $3$ are there?

callout.title: Key takeaway
callout.text: Focus on the core idea in MCQ - Permutations of Size 3 and choose an implementation that remains correct on edge cases and within the stated complexity.

pages.title: Calculating number of permutations
pages.content:
Let's see these permutations as arrangements of $N$ items. Initially all the $N$ places are empty and we will go serially and arrange number from $1$ to $N$ in these $N$ places.

First we have to arrange (or place) $1$, currently there are $N$ empty places (or choices).\
Now, we will place $2$, currently there are $N - 1$ empty places (or choices). \
Now, we will place $3$, currently there are $N - 2$ empty places (or choices). \
.\
.\
At last we will place $N$, there will be only $1$ empty place (1 choice).

No matter which place you choose for a particular numbers, the upcoming numbers will have the same number of choices (empty places to choose from). \
Since choices are independent, we will use the rule of product here. 

Number of choices while placing $1$, $N$.\
Number of choices while placing $2$, $N - 1$.\
.\
.\
Number of choices while placing $i$, $N - i + 1$.\
.\
.\
Number of choices while placing $N$, $1$.

So the total number of arrangements will be equal to $N$ $\cdot$ $N - 1$ $\cdot$ $.$ $.$ $2$ $\cdot$ $1$.\
In other words - it is equal to product of all integers from $1$ to $N$. \
This is called $N!$, pronounced as N-factorial.

callout.text: Focus on the core idea in Calculating number of permutations and choose an implementation that remains correct on edge cases and within the stated complexity.

pages.title: MCQ - Fruit Arrangement Combinatorics
pages.content:
In how many ways can you arrange $2$ apples and $3$ oranges. All apples are indistinguishable from each other and all oranges are indistinguishable from each other.

1. $5!$
2. $\frac{5!}{2! \cdot 3!}$
3. $\frac{5!}{3!}$
4. $\frac{5!}{2!}$

callout.title: Key takeaway
callout.text: Focus on the core idea in MCQ - Fruit Arrangement Combinatorics and choose an implementation that remains correct on edge cases and within the stated complexity.

pages.title: Combinations
pages.content:
A combination is a selection of items from a set that has distinct items. 

If the number of items is $N$ and you have to select $K$ of them, then the number of ways is defined by the function $^NC_K$. 

$^NC_K$ is defined as $\frac{N!}{K! \cdot (N - K)!}$.

Why? we can arrange the $N$ items in $N!$ ways and then pick starting the $K$ elements of the bunch. \
But, since we do not care about he arrangement of first $K$ elements and the last $N - K$ elements, we remove the arrangements of these items.

For example, if you have $4$ fruits and you want to pick $2$ of the fruits, this can be done in $\frac{4!}{2! \cdot 2!}$ $=$ $6$ ways.

What if we want to select $K$ items from a set of $N$ distinct items and arrange them too, how many ways can we do this? 
- First pick $K$ elements from the bunch, this can be done in $^NC_K$ ways.
- Now, arrange the $K$ picked elements in $K!$ ways.
- Since these two are independent actions, use the rule of product and get, $\frac{N!}{ (N - K)!}$.

We define another function $^NP_K$ $=$ $\frac{N!}{ (N - K)!}$, the number of permutations of $K$ elements, selected from a bunch of $N$ elements.

pages.title: Concept  - Combinatorics
pages.content:
Let's say that we have characters $C_1$, $C_2$, ..., $C_n$ with frequencies $F_1$, $F_2$, ... $F_N$ respectively.

Let the length of the string we are constructing be $Len$.

Now imagine constructing the string by placing the characters serial-wise. \
First we will place character $C_1$, we have $Len$ places. (Say - stage 1)\
Then, we will place character $C_2$, we have $Len$ $-$ $F_1$ places. (Say - stage 1) \
. \
. \
At last, we will place the character $C_N$, we will have $Len$ $-$ $\sum_{i = 0}^{N - 1} F_i$ places. (Say - stage N)

Notice that at every stage (say $k$), we will have $Len$ $-$ $\sum_{i = 0}^{k - 1} F_{i}$ number of places to fill; irrespective of how we have filled the characters at previous stages.

So these actions are Independent - we will apply the rule of product here.

pages.title: MCQ - Permutation Subsequence Calculation
pages.content:
Let's say a number $x$ appears $f[x]$ times in the array $A$. \
In how many ways can you form a permutation subsequence of size $L$?

Option 1: $\prod_{i=1}^L (f[i] + 1)$ 

We are increasing the frequency of each element by 1 and then multiplying it with the frequencies of the other elements, which are also increased by 1.

Option 2: $\prod_{i=1}^L f[i]$ 

We are taking the frequency of each element and then multiplying it with the frequencies of the other elements.

Option 3: $1 + \prod_{i=1}^L f[i]$ 

We are taking the frequency of each element, multiplying it with the frequencies of the other elements, and adding 1 at last.

Option 4: $\sum_{i=1}^L f[i]$ 

We are adding the frequency of all the element.

callout.title: Key takeaway
callout.text: Focus on the core idea in MCQ - Permutation Subsequence Calculation and choose an implementation that remains correct on edge cases and within the stated complexity.

pages.title: Concept - Optimizing Permutation Calculation
pages.content:
So now we need to simply find number of ways we can form all the permutation from size $1$ to $N$.

This is equal to 
$$
\sum_{L = 1}^N (\prod_{i = 1}^L f[i])
$$

To optimize it, note that that we’re essentially taking prefix products of the $\text{f}$ array, and all of those can be computed in $\mathcal{O}(N)$ time total once $\text{f}$ is known, thus solving the problem in $\mathcal{O}(N)$.

callout.title: Key takeaway

pages.title: MCQ - Stone Color Patterns
pages.content:
Which of the following will hold true?
1. For $i > K$, stone $i$ will have same colour as stone $i - K$.
2. If paints of all the stones from $1$ to $i - 1$ are fixed, then $i$-th stone can be painted in $K$ ways
3. For $i > K$, stone $i$ will have same colour as stone $i - 2 \cdot K$.
4. None of these.

callout.title: Key takeaway
callout.text: Focus on the core idea in MCQ - Stone Color Patterns and choose an implementation that remains correct on edge cases and within the stated complexity.

pages.title: Concept - Coloring Stones Combinations
pages.content:
Let’s try to color the stones one at a time, from $1$ to $N$.

- Stone $1$ can be colored in any of the $K$ colors, there are no restrictions yet.
- Stone $2$ has $K-1$ options, since it can’t be the same color as $1$.
- Stone $3$ has $K-2$ options, it can’t be the same color as the previous two.
- $\vdots$
- Stone $K-1$ has $2$ options.
- Stone $K$ has $1$ option, since it can’t be any of the previous $K-1$ colors (which are all distinct).
- Stone $K+1$ has only one option: it can’t take the color of any of stones $2, 3, \ldots, K$; but it can take the color of stone $1$.
- Similarly, stone $K+2$ must have the same color as stone $2$, and so on.

In general, if $i \gt K$ then stone $i$ will have exactly one option: have the same color as stone $i-K$.

callout.title: Key takeaway
callout.text: Focus on the core idea in Concept - Coloring Stones Combinations and choose an implementation that remains correct on edge cases and within the stated complexity.

pages.title: Concept -  Stone Painting Choices
pages.content:
If $K \leq N$, answer will be $K!$ as all stones $i \gt K$ will have one choice.

If $K \gt N$, then first stone paint will have $K$, second $K - 1$, ...., $N$-th stone will have $K-N+1$ choices. \
So the answer will be $K\times (K-1) \times \ldots \times (K-N+1) = \frac{K!}{(K-N)!}$

callout.title: Key takeaway
callout.text: Focus on the core idea in Concept -  Stone Painting Choices and choose an implementation that remains correct on edge cases and within the stated complexity.

pages.title: MCQ - Paths Combinations
pages.content:
We make exactly $2N - 2$ moves, $N - 1$ are "right" moves and the other $N - 1$ are "down" moves. \
We want to align these moves such that there are exactly $K$ "turn" cells, meaning - we reach the cell with a move different than we leave the cell.

If we fix the first move to "right", in how many combinations can we reach the last cell.

1. $$
^{N - 2}C_{\lfloor\frac{K}{2}\rfloor} \cdot ^{N - 2}C_{\lfloor\frac{K - 1}{2}\rfloor}
$$

2. $$
^{N - 1}C_{\lfloor\frac{K}{2}\rfloor} \cdot ^{N - 1}C_{\lfloor\frac{K - 1}{2}\rfloor}
$$

3. $$
^{N}C_{\lfloor\frac{K}{2}\rfloor} \cdot ^{N}C_{\lfloor\frac{K - 1}{2}\rfloor}
$$

4. None of these

callout.title: Key takeaway
callout.text: Focus on the core idea in MCQ - Paths Combinations and choose an implementation that remains correct on edge cases and within the stated complexity.

pages.title: Concept - Path Counting Formula
pages.content:
Now if we make the the first move "down", we will have the same scenario as the previous one but rotated. 

So in this case, the answer will still be  
$$
^{N - 2}C_{\lfloor\frac{K}{2}\rfloor} \cdot ^{N - 2}C_{\lfloor\frac{K - 1}{2}\rfloor}
$$
